transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, what brings me in is… I’ve been noticing this thing where people will be talking right to me, and I’m looking at them, you know, I’m not trying to ignore them or anything, but then I realize I didn’t really catch part of what they said.

Like at the museum, when we’re talking about the next art walk, someone will be explaining something to me — what time we’re meeting, or who’s doing what, or whatever the plan is — and I’ll be standing there looking right at them, nodding along even, and then it’s like the middle of the sentence just disappeared. I’ll catch the beginning and the end, but not the important part in between. Then I have to ask them to run it by me again, which feels a little embarrassing, especially when it’s clear they were speaking directly to me.
Can you tell me more about these moments when you miss part of what someone is saying? Are you often distracted during conversations, or do you notice your mind wandering at those times?

Yeah, I’d say it’s more like my mind sort of slips away for a moment, even though I’m trying to listen. It’s not like I’m turning my head and looking at something else, or purposely tuning the person out. I’ll be right there in front of them, making eye contact, nodding, and I think I’m following along.

But then, especially at the museum when we’re talking about the next art walk, someone will be telling me the plan — like where we’re supposed to meet, or what time, or who’s handling which part — and I’ll suddenly realize I caught the start of what they said and then the end, but the middle is just… gone. And usually the middle is the part I actually needed.

So then I have to say, “Sorry, can you run that by me again?” And I feel bad because they were talking right to me. It’s embarrassing, because from the outside I probably look like I heard it all. I don’t always know what distracted me, either. Sometimes it’s just like I drifted without meaning to.

Besides missing parts of conversations, have you noticed any other changes in how you think or remember things lately? Like forgetting appointments, losing your train of thought, or having trouble organizing your ideas?

Yeah, the main other thing I’ve noticed is with reading through things or trying to stay with written material. Like if I sit down with a gallery packet, or even just a set of notes about something we’re planning, I can start out okay. The first paragraph or so, I’m there, I’m reading it, I understand it.

But then after a few minutes, I’ll realize my eyes are still moving across the page like I’m reading, but my mind has sort of gone somewhere else. And then I have this moment where I think, wait, I don’t actually know what that last part said. So I have to go back and read the same section again, sometimes more than once.

It’s frustrating because it’s not that the material is too hard, necessarily. It’s more like I can’t keep my attention pinned to it for very long. I’ll be physically sitting there with the packet in front of me, doing the right thing, but mentally I’ve drifted off without noticing right away. Then I lose time rereading, and I feel kind of foolish because I was looking right at the page the whole time.
Do you find it hard to stay focused on tasks that require sustained attention, like following directions or finishing work, even if they’re not reading-related?

Yes, I do notice that with things people ask me to do, especially if it’s more than one step. It’s not so much that I refuse to do it or I don’t care — I usually mean to do the whole thing. But if someone from the volunteer group says, you know, “Can you print the maps, call the museum desk, and get the folders ready,” I might start off fine. I’ll print the maps, and I’ll feel like I’m on track.

But then somehow the next part doesn’t happen right away. I might forget to call the museum desk, or I’ll start putting the folders together and then leave them sort of half-ready, like the papers are there but not actually organized or finished. Then later someone says, “Did you ever call?” or “Are those folders ready?” and I get that sinking feeling, because I really did intend to finish it.

It’s embarrassing because these aren’t complicated things. It’s just when there are a few pieces to keep in mind, I can do the first one and then sort of lose the thread unless someone reminds me.
Do you often feel restless or find yourself needing to be constantly moving, especially in situations where you're expected to sit still, like during meetings or while reading?

I’m not sure I’d say that’s a big thing for me, no. I mean, I can get uncomfortable sitting for a long time the way anyone might, especially if a chair is hard or a meeting drags on, but I don’t really feel like I have to be up and moving all the time.

When I’m reading, it’s more that I might lose focus, but I’m not usually pacing around or feeling like I can’t stay in the seat. And in meetings, I might shift around a bit or adjust myself, but I don’t think people would describe me as restless or constantly moving. At least, I haven’t noticed that as the main problem.
Have you noticed any times when you feel like you're acting without thinking, interrupting others, or having a hard time waiting your turn, especially in group settings or conversations?

No, I don’t think that’s really something I’ve noticed much. I mean, I might occasionally speak up at the wrong moment like anyone does, especially if I’m worried I’ll forget what I was going to say, but I wouldn’t say I’m usually interrupting people or blurting things out without thinking.

In group settings, I’m more likely to kind of hang back and listen, or at least try to follow what’s being said. Waiting my turn isn’t usually the problem. If anything, I may miss the moment to say something because the conversation has moved on. But acting impulsively or not being able to wait — no, that doesn’t feel like one of the main issues for me.
